ngram.basis: dev split of the seed 20260825 corpus, calibrated n-gram engine

llm.basis: not a boundary: the self-reported scale decides nothing (spec section 12.1)

note: One block per engine, because one number cannot serve two scales.
The rule engine's confidences are NOT measured and are NOT probabilities. They are
the rule-tier band mapping spec section 11.3 asks for in its last paragraph, so that
the decision procedure has one shape across both engines. The rule engine reports one
of four ordered tiers, whose values are tier_values above and are stated in
classify/base.py. tau_high sits at the MEDIUM tier value, so HIGH and MEDIUM both land
in the confident band; tau_low sits at the LOW tier value, so a context-only match
lands in the low band and becomes a note; NONE falls below both and the tool says
nothing.
Why MEDIUM is confident rather than low. MEDIUM is what an identifier, a
placeholder, or an option list earns. A name attribute reading cardnumber and a
select offering twelve months are strong, checkable evidence about a control, and
they are the only evidence a hostile page leaves standing. Putting them in the low
band would mean the tool could never say anything above a note about exactly the
pages it exists for. LOW is context only, which is prose near the control rather
than anything on it, and that genuinely is a near miss worth a note and no more.
The rule block's four measurement keys stay null and always will. Nothing about the
tiers has been measured, and a plausible number sitting in a file the runtime reads
would be a law 3 violation with a straight face. The n-gram block, added when the
derivation of spec section 11.3 runs, is where measured numbers live, because the
n-gram engine is the one whose confidences are calibrated probabilities that a
precision target can be computed against.
An engine with no block here is an error rather than an inheritance. Applying one
engine's boundary to another engine's confidences would be applying a scale to
numbers produced on a different one, and it would do it silently.
The llm block, added at P6, is the one block whose two numbers are not a boundary.
Spec section 12.1 says a self-reported confidence never feeds the threshold policy of
spec section 11.3, and the decision procedure in audit/engine.py is engine-agnostic by
confidence value: it compares prediction.confidence against tau_high whatever produced
it. So the engine needs two floats and must not be gated by them, and the only pair
that satisfies both is zero and zero. They were pre-registered in
experiments/predictions/p6-llm-comparison.md before the engine classified a field.
Two consequences, stated here rather than discovered later. The language model gets no
threshold protection: every committed prediction with a declaration becomes an
accusation, where the n-gram engine's accusations are gated by a boundary derived
against a 0.98 precision target. A finding-level precision comparison between the two
is therefore not a comparison of two classifiers, and the sentence saying so travels
with the table. And LOW_CONFIDENCE is unreachable for this engine, because tau_high
fires first on every field; an engine whose confidence is not a scale cannot have a
band partway along it.
Deriving a boundary on the self-reported scale against a precision target, the way P4
derived the n-gram engine's, was rejected in advance rather than after seeing whether
it would have helped. It is the thing spec section 12.1 forbids, and that it would
probably raise the language model's finding-level precision is the reason to refuse it
before the measurement rather than a reason to reconsider after one.
